source.version: arXiv 2504.13868 author manuscript, retrieved from the unversioned URL arxiv.org/pdf/2504.13868 (retrieval.json). The document prints no arXiv version number or date. Page 1 reads '(accepted and forthcoming in Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans)'. Not the journal's typeset version of record (DOI 10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100289, per the search record). The search record lists an arXiv v1 titled 'Using Generative AI Personas Increases Collective Diversity in Human Ideation'; this file carries the later title, so it is not v1.
source.title_on_document: Diverse AI Personas Can Mitigate the Homogenization Effect in Human-AI Collaborative Ideation

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials appended to this PDF, pp. 28-53 (table of contents on p. 28).
supplement.holds: Persona taxonomy, prompts and sample plots (pp. 29-38); Table S1 per-persona similarity and distinctiveness (p. 39); Figures S1-S3 (pp. 40-42); recruitment and random-assignment text and interface screenshots for each condition, including the verification question after the 0-plot condition (pp. 43-51); Table S2 Bayesian model summary and equivalence tests (p. 52) and Bayes factors (p. 53); Table S3 condition means without SDs, Cohen's d for each pair of conditions, ANOVA effect size and power analysis (p. 53). The frequentist estimates with standard errors are in main-text Tables 2-4; the main text (pp. 14-15) prints rounded versions of the Bayesian and Cohen's d values that Tables S2-S3 print in full. The full list of 300 plots is 'available from the corresponding author' (p. 31).

paper_design_summary: Phase 1 (model only): ten GenAI personas, built with ChatGPT o1-preview, each generated 30 three-sentence plot ideas with GPT-4o (300 plots), and the authors compared ada-002 embedding similarity within and between personas and against 30 plots from Doshi and Hauser's (2024) prompt. Phase 2: 100 UK Prolific participants were randomly assigned to write an eight-sentence story about an adventure on another planet with no AI (0-plot), with the option to request one plot idea (1-plot), or with the option to request up to five (5-plot), each drawn at random from the 300 persona plots. After 3 control exclusions, 97 stories were analyzed for similarity across writers with ada-002 embeddings (to the condition centroid and pairwise) and for NLTK word counts, whose printed groups do not match the assigned arms; creativity was not rated.

studies.label: Phase 1: diversity of plot ideas from 10 GPT-4o personas (model only)

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people assigned. Ten personas, each combining randomly sampled traits from 14 categories, were each prompted with GPT-4o to write 31 plot ideas, of which the first 30 were kept (300 in all). A comparison set of 30 plots used Doshi and Hauser's (2024) prompt on GPT-4.
assignment.quote: We developed 10 distinct GenAI personas using ChatGPT's o1-preview model through a systematic, multi-stage process designed to maximize diversity across multiple dimensions.

participants.who: No human participants. The units are 300 persona plots (30 from each of 10 personas) and 30 plots from Doshi and Hauser's prompt.
participants.quote: we conducted a comprehensive similarity analysis of the 300 story plots generated by our 10 distinct personas (30 plots per persona)

ai_tool.name_model: Personas created with ChatGPT o1-preview; plots generated with GPT-4o (version 2024-05-13, temperature 0.9, top P 1) on Azure OpenAI; comparison set with GPT-4 on the Azure OpenAI chat playground
ai_tool.how_used: Model-only generation. Each persona was prompted 'Create thirty-one plot ideas of exactly three sentences each that [persona name] would write', and the first 30 were kept. No person uses the model.

task.description: Three-sentence plot ideas for a short story about an adventure on another planet.

outcomes.name: Intra- versus inter-persona similarity of AI-generated plots
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity (x100) of OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embeddings for 4,350 within-persona pairs (435 per persona) and 40,500 between-persona pairs (900 for each of 45 persona pairs) (p. 6). Per-persona distinctiveness = mean intra minus mean inter similarity (Table S1, p. 39). The 30 plots from Doshi and Hauser's prompt give a benchmark intra-group similarity. AI outputs only; no person received AI help, so the construct is 'other', not diversity across people. The printed t (119.9443) does not follow from 4,350 and 40,500 pairs (about 89 to 90 by Welch or pooled t); it fits 8,700 within-persona comparisons, twice 4,350 (outcome-checker arithmetic, confirmed by the finalizer). S1-O1 enters no estimate.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Between-persona plot pairs (inter-persona)
contrasts.control_arm: Within-persona plot pairs (intra-persona)
contrasts.reported: Direction coded on diversity (codebook section 7): between-persona pairs are less similar. Table 1: Mean intra-persona similarity 87.41 ± 3.17; Mean inter-persona similarity 82.93 ± 3.12; Difference 4.49; T-test t = 119.9443, p < 0.00000001; Effect size (Cohen's d) 1.4254; Most distinctive persona Persona 6 (score: 7.69); Least distinctive persona Persona 7 (score: 2.48). Text gives the SDs as SD = 3.17 and SD = 3.12. Pair counts: 4,350 within and 40,500 between (p. 6). Benchmark: the 30 plots from Doshi and Hauser's prompt had intra-group similarity 90.99 (SD = 2.78) (p. 7; Table S1 'D&H simulation'); no test against the persona plots is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 2.3.1 and Table 1; p. 6, Section 2.2; p. 39, Table S1

studies.label: Phase 2: story writing with optional persona-generated AI plot ideas (Prolific)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: 0-plot (no AI support), 1-plot (option to request one AI plot idea), or 5-plot (option to request up to five AI plot ideas); ideas drawn at random from the 300-plot persona pool.
assignment.quote: The participants were randomly assigned to write an eight-sentence short story under one of three experimental conditions
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 3.1; p. 43, Supplementary Materials 'Story writing by participants'

arms.name: 0-plot (control, human only)
arms.description: Wrote the eight-sentence story with no AI support (p. 45); afterwards asked whether they used ChatGPT or a similar generative AI tool to inspire the story (p. 46).

arms.name: 1-plot
arms.description: Same task with a 'Suggest Story Idea' button that shows one GenAI plot idea drawn at random from the 300 persona plots; requesting and using it were optional (p. 11; p. 43; pp. 47-48).

arms.name: 5-plot
arms.description: Same task with five 'Idea' buttons, each showing a GenAI plot idea drawn at random from the 300 persona plots; requesting and using them were optional (p. 11; p. 43; pp. 49-51).

participants.exclusions: Three participants in the 0-plot control group were excluded because they reported using external AI to inspire their stories (p. 11; p. 52). The supplement shows this verification question only after the 0-plot condition (p. 46). Per-arm counts at assignment are not printed. Table S3 labels its block 'Intent-to-Treat Analysis' but reports 'Achieved Power (n=97)', so the analysis does not keep everyone assigned.
participants.who: UK-based Prolific workers with an approval rating at or above 95 percent and between 100 and 1,000,000 prior submissions (same criteria as Doshi and Hauser 2024); over 18; paid 3 pounds for a study expected to take about 15-20 minutes (p. 44). One story per participant.
participants.quote: After excluding data from three participants in the control group who reported using external AI to inspire their stories, we analyzed 97 stories: 32 in the control group, 33 in the 1-plot condition, and 32 in the 5-plot condition.
participants.locator: pp. 10-11, Section 3.1; p. 43; p. 44 (consent page); p. 13, Table 3 (Count 32 / 33 / 32)

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o (version 2024-05-13, temperature 0.9, top P 1) on Azure OpenAI, prompted with 10 personas created with ChatGPT o1-preview; plot ideas pre-generated in Phase 1
ai_tool.how_used: Plot ideas were pre-generated in Phase 1 (300 plots, 30 per persona). On the writing page, participants in the AI arms could click a button to see one plot (1-plot) or up to five plots (5-plot), each drawn at random from this pool. Requesting and using the plots were optional (p. 11; p. 43). No live interaction with a model. The paper does not report how many participants requested or used plots.

task.description: Write a story about an adventure on another planet, exactly eight sentences long, in English, appropriate for a teenage and young adult audience (approximately 15 to 24 years of age) (pp. 45, 47). The consent page also mentions a prior short task of providing ten words (p. 44), which the paper does not describe or report.
task.duration: Whole study expected to take about 15-20 minutes (consent page, p. 44); story-writing time not stated.

outcomes.name: Story similarity to the condition centroid (replication of Doshi and Hauser 2024)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity (scaled to 100) between each story's OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 embedding and the centroid (average embedding) of all stories in the same condition. Higher means more homogeneous, so the sign is reversed for diversity. One story per participant. Linear regression with the control group as reference (Table 2) and one-way ANOVA across the three conditions (p. 12); arm summary statistics in Table 3.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity (x100) of each story to its condition's centroid embedding
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each story against the centroid (average embedding) of all stories in its own condition
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Linear regression of the 97 story-level centroid similarities on condition dummies, control as reference; the paper does not state the SE type, and Table 2 prints the values in parentheses to one decimal without a label; one-way ANOVA across the three conditions
diversity_detail.notes: Higher similarity = less diverse. Table 2 reprints Doshi and Hauser's (2024) Table S11 estimates beside this paper's: 0.871*** (0.227), 0.718** (0.240), constant 89.961*** (0.161), Observations 293, F-Stat 8.23, Adj R-squared 0.044. Those belong to Doshi and Hauser's sample, not this one.

outcomes.name: Pairwise story similarity within condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity (x100) of ada-002 embeddings for every pair of stories within a condition. Main model, at the pair level: similarity ~ condition + (1|story1_id) + (1|story2_id), REML, 1,520 pairs (496 / 528 / 496) (Table 4); unit and n_units refer to this model. Story-level variant of the same measure: each story's average similarity to all other stories in its condition (97 observations), with one-way ANOVA, post-hoc t-tests and a 10,000-iteration permutation test (pp. 13-14). Table S3's Cohen's d values (p. 53) are story level: at 32 / 33 / 32 stories they give the post-hoc t values 1.88, 1.45 and -0.73 (checker and finalizer arithmetic). The Bayesian hierarchical model (4 chains x 2,000 iterations, ROPE ±0.5, Bayes factors; pp. 14-15; Table S2, pp. 52-53) is not labeled by level; its intercept (82.616, the Table S3 control mean of 82.62) and sigma (1.7, sd 0.126) fit the 97 story averages, not the 1,520 pairs, whose residual variance is 5.45 (arithmetic; open question 11). The 5-plot vs 1-plot contrast has no pair-level estimate. Higher = more homogeneous; sign reversed for diversity.

contrasts.treatment_arm: 1-plot
contrasts.control_arm: 0-plot (control, human only)
contrasts.reported: Direction coded on diversity (codebook section 7): the paper reports similarity, and the 1-plot arm's similarity is lower. Pair level, Table 4 (mixed model on 1,520 pairs): Baseline (Control: 0-plot) 82.699, SE 0.327; 1-plot effect (vs. Control) -1.073, SE 0.458, z = -2.341, p = 0.019*, 95% CI [-1.971, -0.175]; 'Story-level variance' (the random-effect variance) 2.765 (0.212). Text: random effects variance 2.76, residual variance 5.45. Story level (each story's mean similarity to the others in its condition; 97 stories, 65 in this pair), not significant at 5 percent: ANOVA F(2, 94) = 2.33, p = 0.103; 0-plot versus 1-plot t = 1.88, p = 0.064; permutation test (10,000 iterations) p = 0.113, reported once without saying which comparison it tests. Bayesian (level not stated; the estimates fit the 97 story averages, see measure_detail): Table S2 model summary condition[1-plot] mean -0.882, sd 0.419, hdi_2.5% -1.7, hdi_97.5% -0.042; Table S2 equivalence testing mean difference -0.882, 95% HDI [-1.686, -0.042], P(effect in ROPE) 0.181; text mean difference = -0.88, 95% HDI [-1.69, -0.04]; BF01 = 0.548, BF10 = 1.826 (text BF01 = 0.55). Table S3: 1-plot condition (81.74) < control (82.62); story-level 0-plot vs 1-plot Cohen's d = 0.467 (text d = 0.47).

diversity_detail.metric: Pairwise cosine similarity (x100) of story embeddings within a condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of stories within the same condition (496 / 528 / 496 pairs for 0-plot / 1-plot / 5-plot); story-level variant: each story's mean similarity to all other stories in its condition (97 stories)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Pair level: linear mixed model with crossed random intercepts for both stories in each pair, REML (Table 4). Story level: one-way ANOVA and post-hoc t-tests on the 97 story averages, and a permutation test (10,000 iterations). Bayesian hierarchical model (4 chains x 2,000 iterations) whose level is not stated; its estimates fit the 97 story averages (arithmetic)
diversity_detail.notes: Lower similarity = more diverse. The story-level average version is the output-level score of codebook section 11, rule 1; its condition means appear only in Table S3 (control 82.62, 1-plot 81.74, 5-plot 82.00), without SDs. Table S3's Cohen's d is positive when the first-named condition is more similar; the paper does not state the standardizer, but the d values give the story-level t values at 32 / 33 / 32 stories, which fits a pooled story-level SD (arithmetic). The control level differs across models: 82.699 (Table 4 baseline), 82.616 (Table S2 intercept), 82.62 (Table S3).

outcomes.name: Total words per story (NLTK)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: NLTK word-tokenizer count of words in each story; a length measure, not a creativity rating. The codebook has no measure code for a plain text count, so automated_score is the placeholder the forms use for a computed count (as in c035 S1-O10 and c052 S1-O8); it does not mean a creativity scoring model. The paper compares an 'AI-Assisted' with a 'Human' group (Table 5) and a '1-plot' with a '5-plot' group (Table 6) with independent-sample t-tests, and the text says the groups are the conditions (p. 12, Section 3.2; p. 15, Section 3.3.3). Tables 5-6 print means, SDs, t and p but no group sizes. Checker and finalizer arithmetic, not stated in the paper: the printed statistics fit only 41 'Human' and 56 'AI-Assisted' stories and 27 '1-plot' and 29 '5-plot' stories, not the analyzed arms (32 and 65; 33 and 32). If the 97 stories are the analyzed ones, at least 9 'Human' stories come from writers assigned to an AI arm. The contrasts are therefore not randomized as printed and are coded comparison_type other (open question 1).

eligibility.reason: Study S2 (Phase 2): each participant was randomly assigned to no AI (0-plot) or to optional access to one (1-plot) or up to five (5-plot) GPT-4o persona plot ideas (p. 10, Section 3.1; p. 43). Of 100 randomized, 97 people were analyzed (32 / 33 / 32; p. 11; Table 3, p. 13), above 50. Diversity across writers was scored on the stories with ada-002 embedding similarity in the assigned arms (Tables 2-4, pp. 12-14; 496 / 528 / 496 pairs, p. 13), so the study is eligible for across_people. No creativity rating was collected. The with_ai outcomes are NLTK word counts (Tables 5-6, p. 16) whose printed statistics fit groups of 41 / 56 and 27 / 29 stories, not the assigned arms (checker and finalizer arithmetic; open question 1), so they are coded as non-randomized contrasts (comparison_type other) and give no randomized with_ai estimate. Caveats: the 3 exclusions all come from the control arm, and take-up of the plot ideas is not reported. Study S1 (Phase 1) is model only.

one_line_finding: Among 97 analyzed UK Prolific writers (100 randomized), optional access to plot ideas from 10 GPT-4o personas did not raise story similarity: similarity to the condition centroid was 90.588 (no AI), 90.095 (1-plot) and 90.233 (5-plot), F(2, 94) = 0.573, p = 0.57 (Tables 2-3, pp. 12-13), and pairwise similarity was lower, that is diversity higher, in the 1-plot arm (-1.073, 95% CI [-1.971, -0.175], p = 0.019) but not significantly in the 5-plot arm (-0.488, p = 0.291) (Table 4, p. 14).
open_questions: Groups behind Tables 5-6 (p. 16). The paper prints no group sizes and says the groups are the conditions (p. 12, Section 3.2; p. 15, Section 3.3.3). Checker and finalizer arithmetic, not stated in the paper: the six count means give whole totals, and pooled two-sample t-tests reproduce all 14 printed t values within 0.0013, only with 41 'Human' and 56 'AI-Assisted' stories (Table 5) and 27 '1-plot' and 29 '5-plot' stories (Table 6), and the Table 6 means weighted 27 / 29 equal the Table 5 AI-Assisted means. The analyzed arms (32 / 65; 33 / 32) fit neither table. The 14 NLTK contrasts are therefore coded comparison_type other, not as randomized contrasts. How the groups were formed (for example, by whether a writer requested a plot) is not stated; the authors would need to explain it or supply the comparisons by assigned arm.
Take-up of the plot ideas (how many participants in the AI arms requested or used a plot) is not reported, so the AI contrasts are effects of offered access.

Which similarity analysis is primary is not stated. Section 3.2 calls the three approaches complementary; the centroid regression (Table 2) replicates Doshi and Hauser, and the abstract's 'some evidence of enhancement in the 1-plot condition' rests on the pairwise mixed model (Table 4). Codebook section 8, rule 2 for across_people needs a choice.

The story-level one-way ANOVA is F(2, 94) = 2.33, p = 0.103 in the text (p. 13) but 'Observed F = 2.720' in Table S3 (p. 53). Table S3's F = 2.720 and eta-squared = 0.0564 fit 91 residual degrees of freedom, that is 94 observations, while every printed count is 97 (people-checker arithmetic, confirmed by the finalizer).
Table 2 prints the values in parentheses to one decimal (0.5, 0.5, 0.3) and does not label them; exact standard errors for the centroid regression are not given.
Per-arm counts at assignment are not printed; the paper gives only 100 recruited and randomly assigned, 3 control exclusions, and 97 analyzed (32 / 33 / 32).
The supplement shows the verification question about outside AI use only after the 0-plot condition (p. 46), and all 3 exclusions come from the control arm.

Whether the NLTK per-story counts (S2-O3 to S2-O9) count as creativity outcomes under criterion 3: the paper calls them linguistic diversity and richer linguistic features, but they are within-story counts, not creativity ratings. Eligibility does not depend on it, because criterion 3 rests on the embedding outcomes S2-O1 and S2-O2.
The consent page mentions a short task of 'providing ten words based on criteria that will be provided to you' (p. 44); the paper does not describe or report it.

Codebook gap: no measure code fits plain text counts. The form uses automated_score as the placeholder for the word and part-of-speech counts (S2-O3, S2-O6 to S2-O9), as c035 and c052 do, and lexical_overlap for the unique-word count and the stopword share (S2-O4, S2-O5). Review 1 may want a code for text counts (codebook section 6).

The Bayesian model (Table S2, p. 52) is called hierarchical, and the paper does not say whether it was fit to the 97 story-level averages or to the 1,520 pairs. Its intercept (82.616) and sigma (1.7, sd 0.126) fit the story-level averages, not the pairs (checker and finalizer arithmetic), and the S2-O2 record labels it that way.

Version: the file is the arXiv accepted manuscript. The journal version of record (Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans, vol. 8, art. 100289; DOI 10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100289, per the search record) is the latest version under codebook section 2 and is not on file. It may correct the printed inconsistencies in open questions 1, 4 and 5.
notes: Version on file is the arXiv author manuscript marked accepted at Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans; the journal version of record may differ. Supplementary Materials (pp. 28-53) are in this PDF. No preregistration, data or code link; the full plot list is 'available from the corresponding author' (p. 31). The paper collects no creativity ratings: 'our study focuses only on the mitigation of the homogenization effect' (p. 22), and whether Doshi and Hauser's individual creativity gains hold 'remains an important question for future research' (p. 23). Directions for similarity outcomes are coded on diversity (codebook section 7), so lower similarity in an AI arm is 'treatment_higher'. Contrasts of 1-plot or 5-plot with 0-plot are ai_vs_bau because the control had no AI. The persona-diversified AI input is the paper's own configuration; its contrast with uniform-prompt AI exists only across studies, through Doshi and Hauser's (2024) estimates reprinted in Table 2. Post-hoc power was 55.4 percent (Cohen's f = 0.244), and the authors estimate about 165 participants for 80 percent power (p. 15; Table S3, p. 53). Centroid similarity levels (Table 3, about 90.6) differ from pairwise similarity levels (Tables 4 and S3, about 82.6) because they are different measures. Phase 1 numbers are in S1-O1. The 14 NLTK contrasts (S2-O3 to S2-O9) are coded comparison_type other, because their printed statistics fit groups of 41 / 56 and 27 / 29 stories rather than the assigned arms (open question 1), so S2 enters the atlas through its across_people outcomes only. The NLTK counts use automated_score as the placeholder code for a computed count, and lexical_overlap for the unique-word count and stopword share (open question 10).

open_items.item: Groups behind Tables 5-6 (open question 1): the printed statistics fit 41 / 56 and 27 / 29 stories, not the assigned arms, so the 14 NLTK contrasts are coded as non-randomized; how the groups were formed is not stated. Eligibility rests on S2-O1 and S2-O2, which compare the assigned arms (32 / 33 / 32 stories; 496 / 528 / 496 pairs).
Take-up of the plot ideas is not reported, so the AI contrasts are effects of offered access (open question 2). Criterion 1 concerns random assignment of access, which the paper states twice.

Primary similarity analysis not named (open question 3): codebook section 8, rule 2 needs a choice between the centroid regression (Table 2) and the pairwise mixed model (Table 4). Both are recorded, so this is an extraction decision.
Story-level ANOVA F = 2.33 in the text but 2.720 in Table S3, whose F and eta-squared imply 94 observations (open question 4). If the journal version does not fix it, the authors.
Table 2 prints the centroid-regression values in parentheses to one decimal and unlabeled (open question 5). If the journal version does not give exact SEs, the authors.
Per-arm counts at assignment are not printed (open question 6); 100 randomized and 97 analyzed (32 / 33 / 32) are.
The outside-AI verification question appears only after the 0-plot condition, and all 3 exclusions come from the control arm (open question 7).
Whether the NLTK counts are creativity outcomes under criterion 3 (open question 8). Criterion 3 rests on S2-O1 and S2-O2.

No codebook measure code for plain text counts (open question 10); a Review 1 codebook decision.
